problems.description: 30 convention violations (score 0.78) across the new files: non-PascalCase classes in app.py and config.py, a non-snake_case function and non-PascalCase class in __init__.py, and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in __init__.py, broker.py, config.py, persistence.py, and registry.py
ClientRegistry guards the registry with a blocking threading.Lock used from asyncio code paths; the docstring argues this is deliberate, but it can briefly block the event loop on contention
send_to silently swallows ConnectionClosed, making dropped deliveries indistinguishable from successful ones
No tests introduced in this greenfield commit for the message schema validation or routing logic

strengths: Clean single-responsibility layering (messages schema / registry / server)
Typed Message dataclass with explicit from_json/from_dict validation and clear MessageValidationError types
Thread-safe registry with a minimal, well-named API (add/remove/get/all_ids/count/__contains__)
Explicit __all__ exports in the package __init__
Health endpoint served on the websocket port via process_request, avoiding a redundant web framework dependency
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-layered greenfield notification server that establishes sound patterns (typed message schema, thread-safe registry, single-responsibility modules) but is held back by 30 naming-convention violations (0.78) and the absence of any tests.

problems.description: Subscribe/unsubscribe control messages ride the same Message type and payload envelope as data messages, coupling protocol control-plane traffic to the data-plane schema; acceptable but a dedicated control message type would separate concerns.

New /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers endpoints expose subscription state with no auth, consistent with the existing /health pattern (demo server), but noted for parity with the pre-existing HTTP surface.

Mechanical convention score (0.78, 30 violations) is repo-wide and dominated by pre-existing files outside this diff (app.py, broker.py, config.py, persistence.py); the code actually added here is convention-clean, so this is a measurement-scope discrepancy, not a commit regression.

strengths: ChannelRegistry mirrors ClientRegistry's lock discipline and API shape, so it slots cleanly into the existing registry pattern.
Message schema change is backward compatible: optional channel field, validated in from_json, only serialized when present.
unsubscribe_all correctly collects emptied channels before deleting (no dict-mutation-during-iteration), and subscribers() returns a deterministic sorted list.
Repeated HTTP response construction is factored into _json_response, removing duplication across the health/channels endpoints.
Proper validation (channel must be a string when present) keeps malformed messages from reaching the fan-out path.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent feature addition that extends the notification server with thread-safe channel subscriptions while mirroring existing registry and HTTP-endpoint patterns and keeping the message schema backward compatible; the 0.78 convention score reflects repo-wide pre-existing violations rather than this diff's own code.

problems.description: RedisBroker._listen is a fire-and-forget background task with no error handling: if the handler raises or the Redis connection drops, the delivery worker dies silently and the message backbone stops delivering until stop() (which would then re-raise the stored exception) — no reconnect logic.
Presence/subscription state is duplicated across in-process ClientRegistry/ChannelRegistry and RedisClientState; every subscribe/unsubscribe/connect/disconnect must update both, creating drift risk.
store.save() and broker.publish() are non-transactional: a crash between the SQLite write and the Redis publish persists history for a message that was never delivered.
Tests cover happy-path pub/sub via fakeredis but none exercise broker failure modes (connection loss, handler raising) that would surface the unhandled-task bug.

strengths: Coherent multi-instance architecture: Redis pub/sub backbone + SQLite history + Redis presence, all cleanly composed into the existing server lifecycle
Dependency-injection seams (injectable broker/client/store) enable both isolated and cross-instance tests via a shared fakeredis FakeServer
Comprehensive docstrings explaining the why (backbone, per-instance delivery, restart survival) and proper async lifecycle management (start/close with cancellation)
Good test coverage added in-commit (broker, persistence, state, server, cross-instance delivery)
Bounded HTTP query parsing for /messages (limit clamped, offset sanitized) and centralized env-driven config
Preserves existing patterns: build_server/run/main structure, __init__ export style, message-envelope routing
commit_reviews.summary: Cleanly engineered integration commit (Redis pub/sub backbone + SQLite history + Redis presence) with strong DI/testability seams and good tests; convention analyzer's 0.78 reads pessimistic — the listed violations (UPPER_CASE constants, PascalCase classes, files outside this commit like app.py/registry.py) are largely false positives against code that actually follows the conventions, so I rate adherence ~0.85 with the only real gap being broker resilience (unhandled background-task failures, no reconnect).

problems.description: transport_name()'s docstring names 'sse' and 'polling' as selectable TRANSPORT values, but only the WebSocket transport is implemented — the API promises backends that don't exist yet.

NotificationServer.handler/process_request still accept connection/request as Any and just forward to self.transport; a Protocol type for BaseTransport would make the seam contract explicit instead of duck-typed.

Mechanical convention score (0.78, 30 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (app.py, broker.py, persistence.py, registry.py); the new code itself (BaseTransport, build_transport, DEFAULT_TRANSPORT) is naming-compliant.
Commit message '[story] Session 4: refactor' is terse; the diff is substantial (transport extraction, new files) and would benefit from a descriptive body.

strengths: Server is cleanly decoupled from websockets: routing logic no longer touches raw connection objects, all delivery goes through self.transport
Follows the established constructor-injection pattern already used for broker/store/state in NotificationServer.__init__
build_transport() factory + env-var selection keeps transport wiring out of the routing logic, preserving config.py's os.environ convention
New public API is consistently exported through __init__.py __all__
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed transport-abstraction refactor that follows the class's existing DI pattern and removes the websockets dependency from routing logic, with only minor seam-typing and aspirational-docstring concerns — though the 0.78 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in untouched files, not this commit's code.

problems.description: Rate limiter uses a fixed-window over local time.time(); across multiple server instances with clock skew, window boundaries can shift slightly and over-limit messages still consume an INCR (window is fully consumed by the limit check). Self-expiring keys and atomic incr are otherwise sound.

server.py import `from .config import database_path, message_ttl_days as default_message_ttl_days, rate_limit as default_rate_limit` exceeds conventional line length; would be cleaner split across lines.
RateLimiter.client is typed as `Any`; a concrete Redis client type/protocol would give better static guarantees, though it matches the loose typing used elsewhere in the codebase.

The mechanical convention score (0.78, 30 violations) flags modules mostly untouched by this diff (app.py, broker.py, registry.py) plus generic class/function/constant rules on __init__.py/config.py/persistence.py that the new code does not obviously introduce — suggesting largely pre-existing repo style debt rather than new violations.

strengths: Redis-backed rate limiter is cluster-wide and consistent with the existing RedisClientState architecture; per-window keys self-expire, needing no separate sweep.
New config getters rate_limit()/message_ttl_days() follow the established env-var-with-default pattern and carry clear docstrings.
history() fetches limit+1 rows to derive has_more without a separate COUNT query — a clean pagination design.
_row_to_dict staticmethod refactor removes duplicated row-mapping logic across recent()/history().
delete_expired() is idempotent and lock-guarded, safe under concurrent cleanup tasks.
New code itself is convention-clean: PascalCase class, snake_case methods, UPPER_CASE constants, and type hints on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally strong cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + message retention + history pagination) that faithfully extends existing Redis/SQLite patterns and refactors cleanly; the 0.78 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing repo style debt in untouched files, while the diff's own new code follows conventions well, so I'd weight fit above the mechanical score.

compounding_issues: Dual-path architecture introduced in Session 3 (Redis-present vs. in-process fallback) forced every later feature to implement two code paths — e.g. Session 5's rate limiter needs both a Redis INCR bucket and a local in-memory bucket map, doubling complexity and maintenance surface.

Session 1 fully discarded the seed Todo API (reduced app.py to a 9-line CLI stub); the story is effectively greenfield, so the 'seed' contributed zero reusable seams — though this was not harmful to later sessions.

send_direct has inconsistent semantics: it always returns True when Redis is available (even for a nonexistent target), but returns False when Redis is absent and the target is not local — a behavioral asymmetry that was never reconciled.

The transport abstraction from Session 4 is partial: only WebSocketTransport exists, and the HTTP server remains hardcoded inside NotificationServer, so Session 5's cross-cutting features still route through the concrete HTTP handler rather than the seam.

Rate limiting counts control messages (subscribe/unsubscribe) per minute per client, and the local fallback bucket map only prunes on new traffic — a minor unbounded-growth and policy-granularity smell.
key_decisions: Session 1: full rewrite of the seed Todo app into a clean single-file async WebSocket notification server with a broadcast/direct/system wire format and a thread-safe client registry — a solid, well-seamed foundation.

Session 2: introduced a channel subscription model (channel↔client registries, subscribe/unsubscribe wire types) plus HTTP introspection endpoints (/channels, /channels/{c}/subscribers), fixing the message-addressing model.

Session 3: adopted Redis pub/sub as an optional, non-fatal broker (graceful fallback to in-process delivery on import/ping failure) and SQLite message persistence written before distribution — the pivotal architecture decision that made the service horizontally scalable.

Session 4: extracted a BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport, moving the connection lifecycle into the transport with server-side callbacks — a pure refactor that improved cohesion without changing behavior.

Session 5: added per-client rate limiting (sliding-minute Redis INCR with local fallback), message TTL retention via an hourly cleanup loop, and a /history endpoint with channel/since/limit/has_more pagination.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a clean, testable core; Session 2 extended it coherently with channels and endpoint introspection; Session 3 made a significant integration leap (Redis fan-out, SQLite durability, pagination) with careful graceful-degradation and cross-server tests; Session 4 was the strongest session — a pure refactor that extracted a transport abstraction and added cohesion without any behavior change or regression; Session 5 capped the arc with production-grade cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, retention, history). Tests grew 4 → 6 → 8 → 8 → 10 with every suite green at each commit (final: 10 passed), and each session's code built directly on the prior state rather than reworking it, indicating a steady improvement in both capability and code quality with the only real flat spot being the un-tested refactor session.
